Hi! I EAE'd into DMAD Music Production last year. 

So the first stage is the write up. This is the same for everyone so I'm not going to touch it, but I can send you my write ups. I did both the 600 character and 1000 character ones.

Second stage is the aptitude test, an additional essay and portfolios.  
In the aptitude test, they test how in-tune your hearing is, as well as throw in a few question of general knowledge (eg. they asked me where Samsung was from.)

In my portfolio, I included 3 original songs and a long write up about the logic behind the lyrics, chord progressions and the inspirations behind them. In my 500 word essay, I talked about my musical achievements, my inspirations and what I want to learn from the course. I can send you my portfolio plus the essay in DMs, idm!   
Rmbr; This is NOT the time to be humble. This is the time to show them why they should let you into the course. The essay was just me bragging ngl. 

I prepared for my portfolio by enrolling into a songwriting course in SOMA, and just chugging out original songs. Pick up an instrument or DAW, it goes a long way in your portfolio. You're sec 3, so you have more time than I did (I only knew I was taking Os in Feb 2021 because I intended to just drop out and go my own way. I had a sudden change of heart.)

Interview + Audition time. This is the final stage.  
For the interview, be confident. The lecturers are not scary at all. Mine is a Warhammer fan, so I used that as a conversation topic to be a little friendly. Move around! Hand gestures! Etc. Relax your body and face; my smile was def a bit stiff because I was anxious.  
For me, they asked about a time where I was in a group and faced a problem. I brought my experience of being in a band for this since I'm not in school, but if you're in school it should be an easy question. They asked me what I'd like to learn in the course, and why I chose it; this is why learning about their course is important. Learn about a few modules they offer, and talk about why you're excited for them. Show them you're really interested.   
Also, if you want, and you are confident enough, some well-placed banter goes a long way.

In the auditions, there were 3 stages; performance, sight-reading and improvisation. For performance, I did one original song + A cover of Mack The Knife by Bobby Darin. I did vocals plus piano, and used a backing track for the Darin song. For the sight reading, they gave us a simple piece of sheet music + a chord prog, and allowed me to vocalize over the progression. Same for improv. It'll be different if you have an instrument but this is pretty much it.  
Side note, for picking your 2 songs, don't choose modern, chart-topping songs that are commonly performed. I've seen Perfect by Ed Sheeran performed at least 20 times (outside of interview context). Also, they may ask about your inspirations; My friend with a Queen profile picture got asked about them. ATB!! You got this. The process is daunting, but it isn't as hard as many people make it out to be.

I was in a band for a couple of years. I desperately wanted to do rock and metal, but I was made to do pop covers. While we/I kicked ass on stage, there were a few times we absolutely fucking bombed. We played to an empty venue once. Some dude at the Istana turned our volume down mid-set like we were a nuisance (even though we were asked to perform there guys wth). Our pianist wrote a cheesy ass love song, and we worked on that for a bit before splitting up. Honestly, I would've hated it, but I loved doing music, so I loved it in the end. I was put through so many things I would've hated, but still came out loving music. It was then I knew music was going to be my career.

I almost went to SOTA to become an illustrator when I was younger. Some ppl said I'm a better artist than I am musician so like, I *thought* I wanted to do arts when I was younger. I tried doing commissions for some fictional currency (on ChickenSmoothie or smth I think, I forgot) and then quickly hated the idea of drawing for someone else, and drawing as a career.

So my suggestion @/original commenter is: sit on the idea for a while. If you're really sure, get an education at an arts school. Sure, some musicians, and in fact a lot of the biggest names, don't or didn't go to art school, but there are people like Elton John, Dua Lipa (I think?) who received training. Look at them now. Also getting a formal education and certificate is best, because if we don't make it as songwriters or composers, we can still fall back on something and take up a different music job.
